sections.h2: How big is Jefferson County, Georgia, and who lives there?
sections.html:
Jefferson County is wide and sparsely populated: 530 square miles, 526 of them land, with 29.8 people per square mile in 2020. Louisville is both seat and largest city; Avera, Stapleton, Wadley and Wrens complete the five. The legislature established the county on February 20, 1796, per Wikipedia.

Its neighbors are McDuffie, Richmond, Burke, Emanuel, Johnson, Glascock, Washington and Warren. Streams south of a line running southeast from Stapleton, just below State Route 80, empty into the Upper Ogeechee; the small area north of it belongs to Brier Creek and the Savannah system. One county school district covers the whole county. Census 2020 listed no urban population at all, and the median age was 43.4.

Seniors are 22.4% of the population and children 21.3%. QuickFacts lists 5,751 households of 2.58 people, a 21.5% poverty rate, and a bachelor's degree for 13.5% of adults. Employers numbered 326 in 2023, with 4,046 jobs.

sections.h2: What is a Jefferson County house worth, and is the market growing?
sections.html:
Values are low and the headcount is falling. The middle value of an owned home is $105,400 for 2020-2024, and the July 2025 estimate of 15,011 residents sits 4.5% under the April 2020 base.

The county held 18,403 people in 1980 and 16,930 in 2010. The 2020 census found 7,148 housing units, with 13.7% vacant. Competition for a buyer comes largely from other older houses, and one carrying no delinquent years is the easier one to place.

sections.h2: How has Jefferson County's population changed since 1900?
sections.html:
Jefferson County reached its largest count in 1920, with 22,602 residents, after growing from 6,111 in 1810 and 18,212 in 1900. Numbers slid to 17,174 by 1970, edged up to 18,403 in 1980, and have declined at every count since: 17,408 in 1990, 17,266 in 2000, 16,930 in 2010 and 15,709 in 2020.

The July 2025 estimate of 15,011 continues the pattern. A smaller population shows up in the QuickFacts totals for health and connectivity: 18.7% of people under 65 lack health insurance, 93.4% of households have a computer and 83.7% have broadband. Retail sales for 2022 came to $10,893 per person, and the county counted 1,631 nonemployer establishments in 2024.

For an owner, a shrinking market means price expectations should rest on recent local sales and not on the figures of a decade ago. Clean paperwork matters more where buyers are few.

sections.h2: Where do I take Jefferson County tax questions?
sections.html:
The Tax Commissioner takes bills and payments at 736 Peachtree Street, Louisville, GA 30434; call (478) 625-7736, with counter hours of 8:30 to 5:00 on weekdays. Questions about what a parcel is worth go to the Tax Assessor, (478) 625-8209.

  • Tax Commissioner: sends bills for land, business equipment, vehicles, mobile homes and timber
  • Board of Tax Assessors: receives returns, homestead forms and appeals
  • Clerk of Superior Court: its record center supplies warranty deed copies and runs the FANS alerts; the tax site lists the clerk at (478) 625-7922

Millage is decided by the county commissioners and the school board, and the Tax Commissioner has no vote on it.

sections.h2: What happens if I miss the Jefferson County deadline?
sections.html:
Real estate and business personal property are generally due November 15, and the 10% penalty lands once 90 days have gone by. Small homesteaded bills, those under $500, escape it.

Beyond that, the Tax Commissioner may levy on the parcel. The office describes this as a last resort and says it would rather collect another way.

  • Mobile and modular homes show April 1 on one county page and May 1 on another, so ask which one governs you
  • The year's mobile home tax must be fully paid before a location permit is issued
  • Vehicle tax follows the owner's birthday

The tax site also mentions a one-time state homestead relief grant shown as a line on bills for owners with an approved exemption. Rentals and homes without an exemption were left out.

sections.h2: How do returns and homestead applications work in Jefferson County?
sections.html:
Anyone holding taxable property on January 1 files at least one return, during the January 1 to April 1 window. Afterward a real property return rolls forward on its own at last year's value, until you buy more land or build.

Business personal property is handled differently: form PT-50P goes in every year, and items you have sold must be reported or the tax continues. If you file a return that states a lower value and the assessors decline it, that is where your appeal begins.

  • First-time owners take a copy of the warranty deed along to the Tax Assessor's Office
  • The office accepts forms at any time, but one arriving after April 1 counts a year later
  • An approved exemption stays until you move, sell or ask for another kind
  • If it is denied, you must be told and can appeal

When a local exemption is bigger than the State's, the local one prevails. The assessor's office can quote the amounts in force.

sections.h2: How can I appeal a Jefferson County value?
sections.html:
After a notice of changed value arrives, send the Board of Tax Assessors a written appeal. One county page counts 45 days from mailing and another says 30, so follow the notice you hold and file early.

You may argue three things: that the property is not taxable, that the value is wrong, or that it is out of line with similar parcels. Complaints about the amount of tax levied do not count. The assessors review, then answer; a remaining dispute goes to the County Board of Equalization for a hearing, and Superior Court follows. Arbitration substitutes for the board, and the assessors' office explains how to choose it.

sections.h2: Which farm, timber and historic programs apply in Jefferson County?
sections.html:
Working farmland can be assessed at 30% of market value in place of the usual 40%. Conservation use is a second route and values farm, timber, sensitive or transitional land by its present use.

  • Covenant: the owner commits to the Board of Tax Assessors to keep the land in that use for at least 10 years, and applications are due in April
  • Standing timber: untaxed until sold or cut, then taxed at full market value times the millage rate
  • Historic buildings: a register-listed structure and up to two surrounding acres can get preferential treatment

If you own acreage, talk to the assessor before listing so you know what the covenant requires of a new owner.

sections.h2: How do I clear tax before a Jefferson County closing?
sections.html:
Get the payoff figure in writing from the Tax Commissioner, and have it paid at the table. A bill older than 90 days already carries the 10% penalty.

The Clerk of Superior Court runs FANS, a free service you join voluntarily that alerts you when records are filed for your property. Sign up before you list, so a lien cannot appear mid-contract. For an inherited or former rental house, ask for each earlier year's balance by itself.

faqs.q: When is the Jefferson County tax bill due?
faqs.a: Generally November 15 for land, buildings and business property, with a 10% penalty once 90 more days pass.

faqs.q: Which phone reaches the Jefferson County Tax Commissioner?
faqs.a: (478) 625-7736. The office is at 736 Peachtree Street in Louisville and keeps counter hours from 8:30 to 5:00 on weekdays.

faqs.q: Do small homesteaded bills pay a penalty in Jefferson County?
faqs.a: No. The 90-day penalty skips homesteaded property whose bill is under $500.

faqs.q: By what date must a Jefferson County owner apply for homestead?
faqs.a: April 1. The office takes applications through the year, though a later one starts a year after.

faqs.q: Whom do I ask about a Jefferson County value?
faqs.a: Call the Tax Assessor, (478) 625-8209; the Tax Commissioner only bills and collects.
